title: The Late Bakery
premise: Jude Voss, a widowed single parent who runs the last bookshop in fading Millbrook, has trained their heart into a locked room — until they hire Marisol Reyes, a pastry chef opening a bakery in the shuttered train station, as a fake date for the Voss family reunion. What begins as a transaction deepens through late-night baking, shared grief, and a buried town secret: the station's closure twenty years ago was engineered by Jude's own family to seize the land. When the documents surface before the autumn festival, Jude must choose between protecting their family name and giving Marisol the justice she came to find. In the end, Jude testifies at the town hearing, loses the family inheritance but keeps the bookshop, and asks Marisol to stay after the last festival train leaves — and this time, she does.
about_author: F. M. Montrose is the pen name of a former small-town bookseller who spent a decade watching trains stop coming and stories keep arriving. They write romances about people who mistake survival for living, and bake a mean sourdough on weekends.

chapters.title: Closed on Sundays
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. We meet Jude closing the bookshop, dodging their mother's call about the reunion, and lying to their daughter Wren that everything is fine. Establishes the locked-heart philosophy and the town's slow decay. Emotional beat: weary self-containment cracking at the edges.

chapters.title: The Woman at the Station
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She arrives in Millbrook with ovens in a rented truck and a folder of old land records hidden under flour sacks. She leases the derelict station concourse, telling no one why. Emotional beat: purpose disguised as a fresh start.

chapters.title: A Reasonable Transaction
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Over coffee, Marisol proposes the fake date: she needs a town ally; Jude needs a shield for the reunion. They shake hands like it means nothing. Emotional beat: two guarded people mistaking convenience for chemistry.

chapters.title: Reunion, Act One
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The Voss estate: cold marble, colder matriarch Eleanor. Marisol plays the charming stranger while cataloguing portraits and names from her father's old letters. Jude watches her work and feels seen. Emotional beat: performance turning perilous.

chapters.title: Dessert
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. By dessert the fake date has fooled everyone including, alarmingly, themselves. Eleanor corners Jude afterward with a warning about strangers digging into Voss history. Emotional beat: first real flutter, immediately punished by dread.

chapters.title: Flour and Dust
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Marisol renovates the station; Jude brings Wren after school. Wren bonds with Marisol over cinnamon rolls, and Jude panics at how easily the three fit together. Emotional beat: domestic warmth as an ambush.

chapters.title: What Her Father Knew
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She reveals part of the truth: her father was the stationmaster fired when the line closed in 2003; he died broke and blamed. She shows Jude one letter but hides the rest. Emotional beat: trust extended halfway, guilt blooming.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Digging in the bookshop's archive, Jude finds a 2003 ledger suggesting the Voss family lobbied to reroute the rail line — and bought the station land cheap. They hide it from Marisol. Emotional beat: complicity chosen in silence.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A storm knocks out power; candlelit inventory night in the bookshop turns into a near-kiss interrupted by Wren's nightmare. Jude retreats behind the heart-is-a-muscle creed. Emotional beat: longing denied at the door.

chapters.title: Eleanor's Version
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Eleanor summons Jude, admits the family's role obliquely, and offers to fund the bookshop forever if Jude keeps Marisol quiet. The price of survival made explicit. Emotional beat: temptation wearing a mother's face.

chapters.title: The Last Train Out
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol finds the remaining letters missing from her office — Jude's handwriting on the sign-out card. She assumes betrayal and buys a ticket home for after the festival. Emotional beat: heartbreak mistaken for proof.

chapters.title: Confession at Closing Time
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude confesses everything: the ledger, the offer, the fear. Marisol doesn't forgive; she asks the question that guts them — 'Did you ever once forget it was fake?' Jude can't answer fast enough. Emotional beat: truth as detonation.

chapters.title: Wren's Map
chapters.summary: Wren's POV (first time). Wren, sensing the fracture, draws a map of 'everyone I love' and leaves it in the shop. Jude finds it and understands what containment has cost their daughter. Emotional beat: innocence as indictment.

chapters.title: The Festival Opens
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Autumn festival begins; the bakery's grand opening doubles as a town gathering. Old-timers trade memories of the station, and Marisol quietly collects testimony. Jude works the crowd as an ally now, not a spy. Emotional beat: fragile alliance rebuilt on shared purpose.

chapters.title: Witnesses
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Three former railway workers agree to speak at the town council hearing. Eleanor's lawyer starts making calls. Marisol realizes justice will cost her the bakery lease. Emotional beat: courage priced in advance.

chapters.title: The Offer Withdrawn
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude refuses Eleanor's money publicly at a family dinner, forfeiting the inheritance and the family's blessing. Eleanor says the sentence Jude has feared all their life: 'You were always your father's child, not mine.' Emotional beat: exile as liberation.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Someone floods the bakery kitchen overnight; the health inspector arrives suspiciously fast. Jude helps salvage what can be saved, and they bake the festival batch in the bookshop's back room, side by side till dawn. Emotional beat: love rekindled in crisis, unspoken but certain.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Climax. At the packed council hearing, Jude takes the stand against their own family, presenting the ledger. Testimony lands; the council votes to reopen the land grant inquiry and restore the Reyes family's claim. Eleanor walks out. Emotional beat: justice outside the law's comfort, inside its process.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The town is divided; some customers boycott the shop. Wren holds Jude's hand through a quiet morning of empty registers. Marisol arrives not with thanks but with bread, and stays past closing without being asked. Emotional beat: cost counted, worth confirmed.

chapters.title: The Last Train Leaves
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Festival's end. Her ticket home sits in her pocket; the restored station platform gleams. Jude meets her there and finally answers the dessert-night question honestly: it stopped being fake at dessert. The train departs empty. Emotional beat: the ask, finally spoken.

chapters.title: Stay
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Resolution. Marisol signs a new lease — the land now hers by right, the bakery reopening under her own name. Jude shelves a new display: local history, front table. Wren adds a fourth figure to her map. Emotional beat: home chosen, not inherited.

chapters.title: Open on Sundays Now
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Jude's POV. Spring. The bookshop and bakery share a doorway; Sunday customers drift between novels and sourdough. Jude reflects that the heart was never a muscle to contain but a door to keep unlocked. Final image: the last train arrives on time, carrying someone coming home. Emotional beat: quiet, earned joy.
